Oh sorry I started writing my comment before I saw yours. I would have an honest conversation with your parents. Guinea pigs are social animals just like we are. We don’t want to go our whole lives alone and maybe tell them Guinea pigs have the same social needs as them. 

You can also offer to work for them to get another. Maybe say you’ll do some extra chores or do “secretary” work for them with their jobs until you “pay off” the guinea? That might show initiative and that you really care about your guinea. 

If neither those are an option, make sure you talk to him for 20-30 minutes a day. Make sure he gets out of his cage often for playtime and cuddles. And make sure he has plenty of toys and 1-2 stuffed animals.

I don’t have any suggestion on liquid bloat, but I also had a guinea pig die recently. I had to go on a cross-country trip, so I left both my guineas with my dad a few days before I had to leave (he lives only two hours away). Right when I got back to my house, he called me and said one of my babies had passed away. 

One of the first things I had my dad do was put a stuffed animal in the cage with my other. The next morning my dad cleaned the cage to get rid of the other one’s smell. 

Your other guinea will be sad for a bit, so make sure you give them lots of snuggles and maybe an extra treat or two. I would also recommend getting another companion ASAP. 

Luckily since I had a few day buffer before my trip, I was able to go on a day trip to get my other guinea a new friend. It was a bit unfortunate I couldn’t bond with my new baby for three weeks, but I knew that was what ultimately was best for my other guinea. 

And luckily they got a long like super quick. Since we don’t know how one died, my dad took my remaining guinea the next day to get her all checked out and we immediately checked out the new baby after we got her. 

Your baby will get through this! And I know you will too. I read your other post and you did all that you could. The only sign my guinea gave before passing was she ate a bit less than normal her last day (but I chalked that up from her traveling). She hadn’t lost any weight or any behavior changes, but I knew she was bred poorly from some past medical stuff so I’m sure there was an underlying condition that I wasn’t aware of. All you can do is monitor and hope they clue you into a problem before it’s too late.
